Diamonds quality

1 The challenge

In this data challenge we explore the qualities of diamonds and their association with price using the ggplot2::diamonds dataset. Recall that, for the three quality variables:

  • best cut is Ideal, worst is Fair
  • best color is D, worst is J
  • best clarity is IF, worst is I1

The task has two parts:

  1. Observe that low quality diamonds (with respect to cut, color and clarity) are, on average, more expensive.
  2. Use models to explain this apparent paradox, and resolve it.

2 Part 1: observing the paradox

If diamonds were priced purely according to quality, we would expect better-cut, better-color, and better-clarity stones to command higher prices. Let’s check that directly.

2.1 Price by cut

ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Price by cut",
       x = "Cut (worst → best)",
       y = "Price (US$)")

Counter-intuitively, Fair cut diamonds (the worst cut) have a higher median price than Ideal cut diamonds (the best cut).

2.2 Price by color

ggplot(diamonds, aes(color, price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Price by color",
       x = "Color (best = D → worst = J)",
       y = "Price (US$)")

The same pattern shows up here: color J (the worst color) tends to be priced higher than color D (the best color).

2.3 Price by clarity

ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Price by clarity",
       x = "Clarity (worst → best)",
       y = "Price (US$)")

Again, I1 (the worst clarity grade) diamonds tend to be priced higher than IF (the best clarity grade) diamonds.

So on all three quality dimensions, the raw data seem to say “worse quality, higher price” — which is the paradox we need to explain.

3 Part 2: explaining and resolving the paradox

3.1 The missing variable: carat

The quality grades are not the only thing that varies across diamonds — size (carat) varies enormously too, and size is well known to be the single biggest driver of a diamond’s price. If low-quality diamonds in this dataset tend to also be larger diamonds, that alone could outweigh the quality discount and make them look more expensive on average. Let’s check whether carat and quality are related.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, carat)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Carat by cut",
       x = "Cut (worst → best)",
       y = "Carat")

This confirms the suspicion: Fair cut diamonds are, on average, noticeably larger (higher carat) than Ideal cut diamonds. This makes sense once you think about how diamonds are cut in practice — it is much harder to cut a large, valuable rough stone into a perfect “Ideal” shape without losing carat weight, so cutters more often compromise on cut quality for big stones to preserve size, while small stones can be cut ideally with little to lose. The same kind of relationship holds, to varying degrees, between carat and color, and between carat and clarity.

So carat is a confounding variable: it is correlated both with the quality grades (worse quality tends to coincide with bigger stones) and, much more strongly, with price. A simple comparison of price across quality groups, without accounting for carat, mixes the (small, negative) effect of quality with the (large, positive) effect of size — and size wins.

3.2 Modeling price as a function of carat

To separate the size effect from the quality effect, we first model how much of price is explained by carat alone, then look at what’s left over (the residuals) once carat has been accounted for.

Price and carat are both strongly right-skewed, and their relationship is multiplicative rather than additive (a diamond’s value scales roughly with a power of its weight), so we work on the log scale, where the relationship becomes close to linear:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1/50) +
  labs(title = "Price vs carat (raw scale)")

ggplot(diamonds, aes(log2(carat), log2(price))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1/50) +
  labs(title = "log2(price) vs log2(carat)")

The log-log relationship is indeed much closer to linear, so we fit a simple linear model of log2(price) on log2(carat):

diamonds2 <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(
    lprice = log2(price),
    lcarat = log2(carat)
  )

mod_carat <- lm(lprice ~ lcarat, data = diamonds2)

summary(mod_carat)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = lprice ~ lcarat, data = diamonds2)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.17606 -0.24456 -0.00853  0.24002  1.93023 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 12.188841   0.001969  6190.9   <2e-16 ***
## lcarat       1.675817   0.001934   866.6   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.3789 on 53938 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.933,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.933 
## F-statistic: 7.51e+05 on 1 and 53938 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The fit is extremely strong (carat alone explains the large majority of the variation in log price), confirming that size is indeed the dominant driver of price.

3.3 Residuals: what’s left after removing the size effect

We now add the residuals from this model back onto the data. A positive residual means a diamond is more expensive than its carat alone would predict; a negative residual means it is cheaper than its carat alone would predict. In other words, the residual is a size-adjusted measure of value.

diamonds2 <- diamonds2 %>%
  add_residuals(mod_carat, "lresid")

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(lcarat, lresid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1/50) +
  labs(title = "Residuals of log2(price) ~ log2(carat)")

With the dominant carat effect removed, we can now ask the original question again, but this time about the residual, size-adjusted price, rather than the raw price.

3.3.1 Residuals by cut

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(cut, lresid)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Size-adjusted price (residual) by cut",
       x = "Cut (worst → best)",
       y = "Residual of log2(price) ~ log2(carat)")

3.3.2 Residuals by color

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(color, lresid)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Size-adjusted price (residual) by color",
       x = "Color (best = D → worst = J)",
       y = "Residual of log2(price) ~ log2(carat)")

3.3.3 Residuals by clarity

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(clarity, lresid)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Size-adjusted price (residual) by clarity",
       x = "Clarity (worst → best)",
       y = "Residual of log2(price) ~ log2(carat)")

The paradox disappears. Once we control for carat, the residuals now behave exactly as intuition expects:

  • Better cut diamonds have higher residuals than worse-cut ones.
  • Better color diamonds have higher residuals than worse-color ones.
  • Better clarity diamonds have higher residuals than worse-clarity ones.

That is, for a given size, higher quality does command a higher price, it was only being masked, in the raw unadjusted comparison, by the much larger effect of carat varying systematically (and inversely) with quality.

4 Conclusion

The apparent paradox — lower quality diamonds appearing more expensive , is a case of confounding, not a genuine quality discount for better diamonds. carat (size) drives the overwhelming majority of a diamond’s price, and in this dataset lower-quality stones tend to be larger stones, because large rough diamonds are harder to cut to a flawless standard without sacrificing carat weight. When we compare raw prices across quality groups we are implicitly comparing diamonds of very different average sizes, so the (large) size effect swamps the (smaller) quality effect and reverses its apparent direction.

By fitting a model of log2(price) on log2(carat) and examining the residuals, the size-adjusted price, rather than raw price, we isolate the quality effect from the size effect. Once this confounder is controlled for, the data show exactly what we’d expect: better cut, better color, and better clarity are each associated with a higher size-adjusted price. The paradox was in the raw comparison, not in how diamonds are actually valued.
